cards.text: Jesus has just bowed His head and yielded up His spirit on the cross (John 19:30). It's the day of Preparation, and the next day is a High Sabbath. The Jews don't want the bodies left on the crosses during the Sabbath, so they go to Pilate, the Roman governor.

cards.question: The Jews ask Pilate to have the ___ broken and the bodies removed.
The soldiers come and break the legs of both men who were crucified with Jesus.

cards.text: The soldiers work their way down the line, and now they come to Jesus. Slow down with me here, friend, because the writer zooms all the way in on this moment.

cards.question: When the soldiers reach Jesus, do they break His legs too?

answers.text: No because He is already dead
Yes just like the other two men

cards.text: Instead, one of the soldiers takes a spear and pierces Jesus' side. Stay right here with me, friend, because what happens next is something the writer wants you to see.

cards.question: When the soldier's spear pierces Jesus' side, ___ and ___ flow out immediately.

cards.text: The writer hits PAUSE on the story right here. “The one who saw it has testified to this, and his testimony is true.”

cards.question: The one who saw the blood and water says he knows he's telling the truth. Why is he telling it?

answers.text: So readers will blame the soldier

cards.text: Then the writer reaches back into the Scriptures, and he doesn't bring just one. He brings TWO.

cards.question: The first Scripture is “Not one of His bones will be broken.” The writer says the soldiers not breaking Jesus' legs fulfills it.
The second Scripture says, “They will look on the One they have pierced.” Which moment at the cross does it point to?

answers.text: The legs of the two men

cards.text: Afterward, a man named Joseph of Arimathea steps forward. He's a disciple of Jesus, but he's been keeping it a secret.

cards.question: Why has Joseph of Arimathea kept it secret that he's a disciple of Jesus?

answers.text: He is afraid of the Jews
He is afraid of the Romans
Jesus asked him to keep quiet

cards.text: Now Secret Joseph walks right up to Pilate and asks to remove the body of Jesus. Friend, I get nervous asking for an extra cookie box, and this man is asking the GOVERNOR.

cards.question: Pilate refuses to let Joseph of Arimathea remove the body of Jesus.

cards.text: Joseph isn't alone. Nicodemus comes too, the Pharisee who had come to Jesus at night back in John 3:1-2, and he doesn't come empty-handed.

cards.question: Nicodemus brings a mixture of myrrh and aloes weighing about ___ pounds.

cards.text: SEVENTY-FIVE POUNDS, friend, and I once tried to lift a tub of cookie dough half that size until my mustache filed a complaint. Then the two men take the body of Jesus and wrap it with the spices, according to the Jewish burial custom.

cards.question: Joseph and Nicodemus wrap the body of Jesus with the spices in ___ cloths.

cards.text: Now, in the place where Jesus was crucified, there's a garden.

cards.question: What is in the garden near where Jesus was crucified?

answers.text: A new tomb where no one had been laid
An old tomb already holding many bodies
A stone room for storing burial spices

cards.question: Joseph and Nicodemus have to carry Jesus far from where He was crucified to find a tomb.

cards.text: With the day of Preparation on them and the tomb close by, they lay Jesus there. Hold that thought, friend, because this story still has more to tell.

findings.problem: The joke 'I get nervous asking for an extra cookie box' doesn't make sense right away. Papa Dorin lives alone on his cookie planet, so it's unclear who he would be asking. The comparison to asking the governor needs explaining before it lands.

rule.text: It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining.

findings.problem: Guessing the weight of the myrrh and aloes is pure luck. Nothing on card 5 or earlier lets a baker reason toward seventy-five pounds. This is one of several discovery questions in stop 2, along with card 2 (why Joseph kept it secret) and card 8 (linen). It could ask something the baker can reason out instead, like what Nicodemus brings the spices for.

rule.text: If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: Stop 1 cards 4 and 6 both end with almost the same hook ('Slow down with me here, friend, because the writer zooms all the way in on this moment' and 'Stay right here with me, friend, because what happens next is something the writer wants you to see'). Cards 8 and 10 use similar 'the writer pauses/reaches' setups. In stop 1, the story cards' voice is mostly these repeated hooks, with no humor or fresh reaction.
findings.question: In a solemn stretch like this, is it acceptable for several story cards to rely on near-identical suspense hooks that add no content, or should each hook be rewritten so it carries the moment differently?
